texts.0: SP, due to insufficient study of the chart features along the planned route, did not recognize most of the ground points near the flight path. SP mismatched prominent linear features with the chart symbology and reported a wrong point on two consecutive legs, and the IP had to take the aircraft and identify the position himself. Basic aircraft control degraded during the search and altitude exceeded 300 ft from the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient study of the chart features along the planned route, failed to recognize confidently the ground points near the flight path. SP identified the required points only after the IP pointed out the reference feature verbally, and the correct position report came at the +/- 300 ft altitude limit while attention stayed inside the cockpit. No IP intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in matching chart symbology with the terrain picture, did not recognize confidently all of the ground points near the flight path on the first attempt. SP re-checked the chart, cross-referenced the surrounding features and identified the point without any prompting, holding altitude within 150 to 300 ft of the assigned value during the search. The recognition was completed early enough to keep the leg timing usable.
texts.3: SP recognized confidently most of the ground points near the flight path and reported them accurately as they passed abeam. SP matched chart symbology with the terrain picture without hesitation and kept altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees while doing so. Position awareness was maintained continuously throughout each leg.
texts.4: SP recognized every ground point near the flight path immediately and reported each one with the correct relative position. SP used secondary features to confirm each identification before calling it, and the basic flight parameters showed negligible deviations throughout. Position awareness remained fully current from departure to the last turning point.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the ground points near the flight path within standards, but the identifications relied mainly on the largest and most obvious features and hesitation was evident on the smaller ones. The trend is toward slower recognition when the terrain picture is less distinctive, and SP is expected to broaden the use of secondary chart features so that recognition remains confident in low-contrast terrain.

texts.0: SP, due to not having internalized the map reading sequence, did not use the right map reading technique and worked from the ground to the map instead of Time - Map - Ground. SP searched the whole chart for whatever feature happened to be visible, lost the running estimate of position and required the IP to intervene and re-establish the navigation picture. Heading wandered beyond 10 degrees from the briefed value during the search.
texts.1: SP, due to not having internalized the map reading sequence, did not apply the Time - Map - Ground technique in the correct order and consulted the chart before checking elapsed time. SP restored the correct sequence only after the IP prompted verbally, and heading was at the +/- 10 degrees limit when the correction started. No control intervention by the IP was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to an unrehearsed cockpit routine, started the map reading cycle from the map rather than from elapsed time on the first two checkpoints. SP recognized the error unprompted, re-established the Time - Map - Ground order and completed the remaining checkpoints correctly, with heading held between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the reorganization. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP used the right map reading technique and worked consistently in the Time - Map - Ground order on every checkpoint. SP checked elapsed time first, narrowed the search area on the chart and then looked out for the expected feature, keeping heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft throughout. The cycle was completed well before each point passed abeam.
texts.4: SP applied the Time - Map - Ground technique on every checkpoint with a fully established cockpit routine and a fixed chart-to-ground scan pattern. SP anticipated each feature before it became visible and confirmed it in a single glance outside, with negligible deviations in heading, altitude and airspeed. The technique was maintained without degradation over the whole route.
texts.marginal: SP used the Time - Map - Ground technique in the correct order and remained within standards, but the sequence broke down briefly whenever two checkpoints came close together. The trend is toward reverting to a ground-to-map search under time pressure, and SP is expected to keep the elapsed-time step first even on compressed legs so that the technique holds at higher checkpoint density.

error_modes.label: TIMELY RECOGNITION OF DEVIATION AND CORRECTION

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete comparison between the observed and the expected ground picture, was not able to recognize timely the developing deviation from the turning point and executed no correction. SP continued on the erroneous picture until the IP identified the deviation and took the aircraft to regain the route. The recovery required a heading change well beyond 10 degrees and an altitude excursion beyond 300 ft.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete comparison between the observed and the expected ground picture, recognized the deviation from the turning point late and executed the appropriate correction only after the IP pointed it out verbally. The correction was initiated with heading already at the +/- 10 degrees limit from the briefed value and the turning point was reached off the planned geometry. No IP control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow first comparison of the terrain picture against the chart, allowed a deviation from the planned track toward the turning point to develop before detecting it. SP identified the discrepancy unprompted, applied a corrective heading and re-established the correct approach to the turning point with heading between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the correction. The turning point was crossed on plan.
texts.3: SP recognized timely the developing deviations from the turning points and executed appropriate corrections in every case. SP compared the terrain picture against the chart early on each leg, applied small corrections before the error could grow and held heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. Every turning point was crossed on the planned geometry.
texts.4: SP detected the first indication of divergence from the planned track well before the turning point and corrected with minimal control input each time. SP anticipated the effect of the wind on the remaining leg and pre-corrected accordingly, leaving negligible deviations at every turning point. No leg required more than a marginal heading adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the deviations from the turning points and corrected them within standards, but the detection came consistently in the second half of each leg rather than early. The trend is toward larger corrections than necessary near the turning points, and SP is expected to start the terrain-to-chart comparison earlier on each leg so that the corrections stay small.

error_modes.label: ATTENTION DIVISION BETWEEN CHART AND AIRCRAFT STATE

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured by the chart while the aircraft state went unmonitored, kept the head down searching for a single ground point and stopped monitoring the flight parameters. The instrument cross-check lapsed completely, altitude departed by more than 300 ft and airspeed by more than 20 kt, and the IP intervened on the controls to restore the aircraft state. Map reading was suspended until the IP handed the aircraft back.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by the chart while the aircraft state went unmonitored, allowed the head-down time on a single ground point to extend well past the time available. SP resumed the cross-check only after the IP called the parameters, with altitude at the +/- 300 ft limit and airspeed at the +/- 20 kt limit at that moment. The correction was completed by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a longer than intended head-down interval on the chart, let the instrument cross-check lapse over one leg. SP recognized the omission unprompted, returned to the scan and corrected an altitude excursion between 150 and 300 ft and an airspeed drift between 10 and 20 kt back to the assigned values. Map reading continued afterwards in short, interleaved glances.
texts.3: SP divided attention correctly between the chart, the outside picture and the flight instruments throughout the navigation. SP kept each head-down interval short and returned to the cross-check between glances, holding altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees. No ground point search was allowed to interrupt the monitoring of the aircraft state.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous cross-check while map reading, with head-down intervals so short that the flight parameters showed negligible deviations at all times. SP timed the chart glances to the quiet parts of each leg and confirmed the aircraft state after every one of them. Attention division remained effective even during the busiest checkpoints.
texts.marginal: SP divided attention between the chart and the flight instruments within standards, but the head-down intervals lengthened noticeably whenever a ground point was not immediately identified. The trend is toward a degrading cross-check under search workload, and SP is expected to break off the chart search at fixed intervals to reconfirm the aircraft state.

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, handled an unfolded and unmarked chart while manoeuvring at the turning point. SP lost the chart orientation completely, was unable to continue the Time - Map - Ground cycle and the IP took the aircraft to stabilize it while the chart was refolded. Altitude and heading exceeded 300 ft and 10 degrees respectively during the episode.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, was still folding and orienting the chart when the next leg had already started. SP re-established a usable chart set-up only after the IP prompted, and heading was at the +/- 10 degrees limit when the leg was finally flown correctly. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a chart folded for the wrong leg, needed additional cockpit time to re-orient the map after the first turning point. SP recognized the problem unprompted, re-folded the chart on the straight portion of the leg rather than in the turn and continued the map reading cycle with altitude held between 150 and 300 ft of the assigned value during the reorganization. The remaining legs were flown with the chart correctly prepared.
texts.3: SP managed the chart efficiently in the cockpit, with the map folded and oriented for the leg in use before each turning point. SP handled the workload on the straight portions of the legs and kept altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees. The map reading cycle was never interrupted by chart handling.
texts.4: SP prepared the chart for every leg in advance and moved through the route without any cockpit handling delay. SP anticipated each turn and completed the chart transition before entering it, leaving negligible deviations in the flight parameters. Cockpit workload remained evenly distributed across the whole sortie.
texts.marginal: SP managed the chart in the cockpit within standards, but the transition to the next leg was consistently completed only just before the turning point. The trend is toward chart handling migrating into the turn as the legs shorten, and SP is expected to complete the chart set-up earlier so that the turning points are flown with no cockpit workload remaining.

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument scan while searching the chart for a ground point, did not maintain the assigned navigation altitude. Altitude departed by more than 300 ft from the assigned value and the trend continued unchecked until the IP intervened on the controls. SP had not recognized the excursion before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument scan while searching the chart for a ground point, allowed the assigned navigation altitude to drift without detecting the trend. Altitude reached 300 ft from the assigned value and SP initiated the correction only after the IP called it verbally. The recovery was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a longer than intended chart glance, let the aircraft drift off the assigned navigation altitude. SP detected the excursion at approximately 200 ft from the assigned value, returned to the scan and regained the altitude promptly and unprompted. The remaining legs were flown within +/- 150 ft.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned navigation altitude within +/- 150 ft throughout the map reading task. SP interleaved the chart glances with the instrument cross-check so that any developing trend was caught immediately. Altitude control remained accurate and prompt on every leg.
texts.4: SP held the assigned navigation altitude with negligible deviations for the entire route, including during the checkpoint identifications. SP corrected the smallest trend before it became a deviation and never let the altitude wander during a chart glance. Altitude control was unaffected by the map reading workload.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the assigned navigation altitude within standards, but a consistent low trend developed during each extended chart glance and was corrected only at the end of it. The trend is toward larger excursions as the map reading workload increases, and SP is expected to reconfirm the altimeter at the end of every chart glance so that the drift is caught earlier.

texts.0: SP, due to power left unadjusted while attention remained on the chart, did not maintain the briefed navigation airspeed. Airspeed departed by more than 20 kt from the briefed value, the leg timing became unusable and the IP intervened to restore the aircraft state. SP had not detected the deviation before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to power left unadjusted while attention remained on the chart, allowed the navigation airspeed to drift from the briefed value. Airspeed reached 20 kt from the briefed value and SP adjusted the power only after the IP called it verbally. No control intervention by the IP was needed and the leg timing was recalculated afterwards.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power adjustment during a checkpoint identification, let the navigation airspeed drift from the briefed value. SP detected the deviation at approximately 15 kt, corrected the power unprompted and re-established the briefed airspeed before the leg timing was materially affected. Airspeed remained within +/- 10 kt for the rest of the route.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within +/- 10 kt while carrying out the map reading task. SP adjusted the power promptly whenever a trend appeared and kept the leg timing consistent with the flight plan. Airspeed control was accurate throughout the navigation.
texts.4: SP held the briefed navigation airspeed with negligible deviations for the entire route. SP anticipated the power requirement at each altitude and configuration change so that no correction was needed at the checkpoints. Leg timing matched the flight plan on every leg.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within standards, but the airspeed decayed slightly on every leg where a checkpoint identification took longer than expected. The trend is toward accumulating timing error over the route, and SP is expected to include the airspeed indicator in the scan between chart glances so that the power is adjusted before the drift develops.

texts.0: SP, due to an unmonitored heading indicator while the chart was in use, did not maintain the briefed heading between checkpoints. Heading departed by more than 10 degrees from the briefed value, the ground picture no longer matched the chart at all and the IP intervened to re-establish the heading. SP had not recognized the divergence before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored heading indicator while the chart was in use, allowed the briefed heading to drift between checkpoints. Heading reached 10 degrees from the briefed value and SP returned to it only after the IP prompted verbally, by which time the expected ground picture no longer matched. The correction was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a relaxed heading hold during a chart glance, drifted from the briefed heading between two checkpoints. SP detected the divergence at approximately 8 degrees, returned to the briefed heading unprompted and re-acquired the expected ground picture on the correct side. Heading remained within +/- 5 degrees on the remaining legs.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed heading within +/- 5 degrees throughout the map reading task. SP referenced the heading indicator between chart glances and applied small corrections before any divergence could develop. The expected ground picture matched the chart on every leg.
texts.4: SP held the briefed heading with negligible deviations across the whole route, including during the checkpoint identifications. SP applied wind corrections that kept the ground picture exactly as anticipated at each point. Heading control was entirely unaffected by the chart workload.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the briefed heading within standards, but a consistent drift to one side appeared during every extended chart glance and was corrected only afterwards. The trend is toward a mismatch between the expected and the observed ground picture on longer legs, and SP is expected to reconfirm the heading indicator immediately after each chart glance.

error_modes.label: USE OF THE CHART AS THE PRIMARY NAVIGATION REFERENCE

texts.0: SP, due to reliance on the automated navigation solution in place of the chart, did not perform map reading and identified no ground points near the flight path. SP flew the route by following the navigation display alone and could not state the position relative to the terrain when asked, so the IP took over the navigation task. The map reading technique was not demonstrated at any stage of the sortie.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on the automated navigation solution in place of the chart, used the navigation display as the primary reference and consulted the map only after the IP directed it. SP then identified the ground points correctly, but each identification came after the point had already passed abeam. No IP control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an early preference for the navigation display, began the route by confirming position from the equipment rather than from the terrain. SP recognized the omission unprompted, reverted to the Time - Map - Ground cycle with the chart as the primary reference and identified the subsequent ground points correctly and before they passed abeam. Basic flight parameters stayed within the limits throughout.
texts.3: SP used the chart as the primary navigation reference and identified the ground points from the terrain picture, treating the on-board equipment only as a cross-check. SP maintained a continuous position estimate independent of the equipment and held altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees. Map reading was demonstrated fully throughout the route.
texts.4: SP navigated entirely by map reading, calling each ground point from the terrain before any confirmation from the on-board equipment. SP used the equipment only to verify what had already been established from the chart, with negligible deviations in the flight parameters. Independent position awareness was maintained without interruption from departure to recovery.
texts.marginal: SP used the chart as the primary navigation reference within standards, but reached for the navigation display first whenever a ground point was not immediately recognized. The trend is toward the equipment replacing the map reading cycle in the harder segments, and SP is expected to complete the Time - Map - Ground cycle before any cross-check with the on-board equipment.

error_modes.label: CHECKPOINT LOOK-AHEAD AND ATTENTION FOCUS DISTANCE

texts.0: SP, due to focusing attention on the ground under the nose instead of on points 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead of the A/C, did not look for checkpoints 2-5 minutes ahead and had none of them identified by 1 minute out. SP started searching for each checkpoint only after it had passed abeam, so the running position estimate was lost over consecutive legs. The IP took the A/C and re-established the navigation picture, with heading already more than 10 degrees off the briefed value and altitude beyond 300 ft from the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to focusing attention too close to the A/C instead of on points 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead, did not have the checkpoints identified by 1 minute out. SP began the ground search only when the point was nearly abeam and reacted in time only after the IP called the look-ahead verbally. Heading was at the 10 degrees limit from the briefed value when the identification was completed, and no control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the chart-to-ground look-ahead, identified the first checkpoints about 30 seconds out instead of 1 minute out. SP recognized the compressed window unprompted, moved the search back to 2-5 minutes ahead and had the remaining points identified on time. Heading stayed between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value while the scan was reorganized, and the leg timing remained usable.
texts.3: SP looked for the checkpoints 2-5 minutes ahead and had them identified by 1 minute out on every leg. SP kept attention on points 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead of the A/C and used one or two prominent points on each leg, holding heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. Each checkpoint was crossed with the position estimate already confirmed.
texts.4: SP maintained the look-ahead window on every leg and had each checkpoint identified well before the 1 minute point. SP anticipated the prominent points before they became visible and confirmed each one with a single glance outside, leaving negligible deviations in heading, altitude and airspeed. The timing crosscheck remained current over the whole route.
texts.marginal: SP kept the checkpoint look-ahead within standards, but the search window shrank toward the 1 minute point whenever a leg contained more than one prominent feature. The trend is toward identifying checkpoints only as they approach the abeam position, and SP is expected to restart the 2-5 minute look-ahead immediately after each point so that the margin does not erode on dense legs.

error_modes.label: SCAN LIMITED TO REFERENCES OFF THE NOSE

texts.0: SP, due to crosschecking the navigation with only references off the nose of the A/C, did not exercise a scan as far as could be seen in each direction. SP disregarded the features abeam and behind the wingline, so a growing offset from the planned track produced no chart-to-ground mismatch and the position could not be resolved. The IP intervened on the controls to regain the route after heading exceeded 10 degrees from the briefed value and altitude departed by more than 300 ft.
texts.1: SP, due to crosschecking with only references off the nose, kept the map reading scan inside a narrow forward sector and did not look abeam. SP located the expected feature only after the IP verbally pointed out a landmark off the wing, and heading was at the 10 degrees limit from the briefed value when the position was re-established. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially narrow forward-only crosscheck, missed the abeam features on the first leg and had to hold the checkpoint identification open longer than planned. SP widened the scan unprompted to include as far as could be seen in each direction and identified the following points from lateral references without delay. Heading remained between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the reorganization of the scan.
texts.3: SP exercised a scan that included as far as could be seen in each direction and did not limit the crosscheck to references off the nose. SP used lateral landmarks to confirm the along-track position on every leg while holding heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. The navigation picture stayed continuous from point to point.
texts.4: SP scanned the full sector on both sides throughout the route and used abeam features as readily as those ahead. SP built each position fix from more than one reference before the checkpoint arrived, with negligible deviations in heading, altitude and airspeed. The wide scan was maintained without any cost to A/C control.
texts.marginal: SP scanned beyond the nose within standards, but the lateral part of the scan was used only after the forward references failed to match. The trend is toward a forward-only crosscheck as workload rises, and SP is expected to include the abeam sector in the routine scan so that lateral landmarks are available before the forward picture becomes ambiguous.

error_modes.label: RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN LANDMARKS FOR CHECKPOINT DISAMBIGUATION

texts.0: SP, due to failing to note the relationship of how landmarks are arranged in relation to one another, could not separate two similar small towns ahead and selected the wrong one as the next checkpoint. SP did not use the surrounding pattern, such as the several towers lying east of one of the cities, to confirm which town was charted as the point. The false fix drove the A/C onto a wrong leg and the IP took the A/C to recover the route, with heading more than 10 degrees off the briefed value.
texts.1: SP, due to treating each landmark in isolation instead of using the pattern formed with the neighbouring features, was unable to decide between two similar checkpoints. SP resolved the ambiguity only after the IP verbally described the relative position of the adjacent features, and altitude had reached 300 ft from the assigned value while the search continued. The recovery was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete reading of how the landmarks are arranged in relation to one another, hesitated between two similar features on one leg. SP unprompted checked the secondary pattern around the point, confirmed the correct checkpoint from the relative position of the surrounding features and continued on plan. Altitude stayed between 150 and 300 ft of the assigned value during the hesitation and was regained immediately afterwards.
texts.3: SP noted the relationship of the landmarks to one another and used it to confirm every checkpoint. SP resolved the similar-looking features by their relative position with respect to the neighbouring towers, roads and water features, while holding altitude within +/- 150 ft and heading within +/- 5 degrees. No checkpoint was accepted on a single feature match.
texts.4: SP read each area as a pattern of landmarks rather than as isolated points and confirmed every checkpoint through at least two relationships. SP dismissed the similar decoy features immediately from their relative geometry, with negligible deviations in the basic parameters. The technique held equally well in featureless and in cluttered areas.
texts.marginal: SP used the relationship between landmarks within standards, but the confirmation came only after an initial single-feature match had already been accepted. The trend is toward mistaking a similar feature for the checkpoint in areas with repeated terrain patterns, and SP is expected to build the identification on the arrangement of the surrounding landmarks before calling the point.

error_modes.label: CHART ALIGNMENT WITH THE ACTUAL TRACK

texts.0: SP, due to holding the chart north-up instead of aligning it in the same relative direction as the A/C's actual track, reversed the left and right sense of the features while flying the reciprocal legs. SP searched for the checkpoints on the wrong side of the course line and rejected the correct features as non-matching, and the along-track position estimate was lost. The IP took the A/C to re-establish the route after heading diverged by more than 10 degrees from the briefed value.
texts.1: SP, due to reading a north-up chart on a southerly leg without aligning it with the actual track, transposed the lateral position of the landmarks with respect to the course line. SP re-oriented the chart only after the IP verbally prompted, and heading was at the 10 degrees limit when the correct picture was restored. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to keeping the chart north-up after the turn onto the reciprocal leg, misplaced the first landmark to the wrong side of the course line. SP detected the inconsistency unprompted, aligned the chart in the same relative direction as the actual track and completed the remaining checkpoints correctly. Heading was held between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the re-orientation.
texts.3: SP aligned the chart in the same relative direction as the A/C's actual track on every leg, including after each turning point. SP read the features on the correct side of the course line without any mental transposition, holding heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. Chart handling did not interrupt the identification sequence.
texts.4: SP kept the chart aligned with the actual track at all times and re-oriented it during the turn so that the new leg was ready before rollout. SP read left and right features directly from the aligned chart with no hesitation, leaving negligible deviations in the basic parameters. Chart orientation remained correct through every course change.
texts.marginal: SP aligned the chart with the actual track within standards, but the re-orientation was performed only after the turn was completed and the first landmark of the new leg was already abeam. The trend is toward a transposed left-right picture in the first part of each leg, and SP is expected to align the chart for the next leg before rolling out of the turn.

error_modes.label: CHARTED ROAD CLASSIFICATION AND ROAD COUNTING
error_modes.source: technique:8.17 CULTURAL FEATURES (Roads, Bridges, Railroads, Power Lines, Populated Areas, Coastal Hydrography)

texts.0: SP, due to counting roads as an orientation technique and trusting the charted road classification, took a two-lane road encoded as primary for the thick single line on the chart and fixed the position on the wrong crossing. SP did not use the planned time of arrival to classify the roads that were seen but were hard to identify, and did not restrict positive road identification to the dual lane highways shown by a double line. The false fix drove a turn onto a wrong leg and the IP took the A/C, with heading more than 10 degrees off the briefed value.
texts.1: SP, due to relying on the charted road classification for a road that was hard to classify from the air, reported the position on the wrong transportation line. SP corrected the identification only after the IP verbally pointed out the dual lane highway as the reliable reference, and heading was at the 10 degrees limit when the correction started. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attempting to separate a primary from a secondary road purely on charted appearance, delayed the time check over the transportation line. SP unprompted used the planned time of arrival to classify the road, confirmed it against the neighbouring double line highway and completed the crosscheck without losing the leg timing. Heading was kept between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the reassessment.
texts.3: SP made no attempt to count roads as an orientation technique and used the dual lane highways, portrayed as a double line, as the reliable transportation references. SP identified the roads that were hard to classify on the basis of the planned time of arrival and obtained accurate time checks along the route, holding heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. Every road crossing used for a fix was positively identified.
texts.4: SP used the transportation lines exactly as the technique prescribes, taking the double line highways as primary references and resolving all ambiguous roads by planned time of arrival. SP obtained crisp time checks at each crossing without any attempt at road counting, with negligible deviations in the basic parameters. Road-based position fixes were correct throughout the route.
texts.marginal: SP used the road network for time checks within standards, but tended to accept the charted classification of two-lane roads without cross-checking it against the planned time of arrival. The trend is toward a wrong fix where several similar roads run parallel, and SP is expected to reserve positive road identification for the double line highways and to time-check the rest.

error_modes.label: POPULATED AREA IDENTIFICATION FROM THE CHARTED OUTLINE
error_modes.source: technique:8.17 CULTURAL FEATURES (Roads, Bridges, Railroads, Power Lines, Populated Areas, Coastal Hydrography)

texts.0: SP, due to attempting to identify a city on the basis of its charted outline alone, matched the built-up area under the A/C to the wrong town and reported a false position. SP did not look for the unique element that differentiates one city from another in the same area and did not allow for the fact that the charted outline excludes the recent suburban developments. The wrong fix was carried into the next leg and the IP took the A/C to recover the route, with heading more than 10 degrees off the briefed value.
texts.1: SP, due to relying on the charted city outline alone, hesitated between two populated areas and reported the checkpoint incorrectly at first. SP accepted the correct town only after the IP verbally named the distinguishing element, and altitude reached 300 ft from the assigned value while the search continued. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to expecting the town to match the size suggested by the chart, was surprised by a populated area much larger than the charted outline and delayed the identification. SP unprompted searched for the unique element that separates that city from its neighbour, confirmed the checkpoint and resumed the planned sequence. Altitude was held between 150 and 300 ft of the assigned value during the delay.
texts.3: SP identified the populated areas by a unique element that differentiates each one from the others in the same area rather than by the charted outline alone. SP allowed for the towns being larger or smaller than the chart suggests, especially the small ones shown by a small circle, and kept altitude within +/- 150 ft and heading within +/- 5 degrees. Every populated checkpoint was positively identified before it passed abeam.
texts.4: SP identified every populated area immediately from its distinguishing element and treated the charted outline only as an indication of where the vertical development of the city lies. SP was not misled by suburban growth beyond the charted outline nor by the small circle symbol used for towns of unknown shape, with negligible deviations in the basic parameters. All city checkpoints were confirmed on first sight.
texts.marginal: SP identified the populated areas within standards, but the identification leaned on the general shape of the built-up area and the distinguishing element was sought only when the shape did not fit. The trend is toward a wrong call where two towns of similar size lie close together, and SP is expected to nominate a unique element for each populated checkpoint during preparation.

error_modes.label: RELIEF INTERPRETATION: CONTOURS, SPOT ELEVATIONS AND MEF
error_modes.source: technique:8.16 RELIEF (Contour Lines, Spot Elevations, MEF, Gradient Tints)

texts.0: SP, due to not taking the contour interval from the chart legend and not using the Maximum Elevation Figures of the grid squares, misread the closely spaced contour lines of a steep slope as gentle rising ground. SP flew the leg without reference to the spot elevations and to the MEF, which already includes 100 to 199 ft of clearance over the highest known feature, and the terrain clearance became the IP's concern. The IP intervened on the controls to climb the A/C after altitude had departed by more than 300 ft from the assigned navigation altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the relief only from the gradient tints and not from the contour lines and MEF, did not anticipate the rising ground on the leg. SP started the climb to restore the assigned navigation altitude only after the IP called the terrain verbally, with altitude at 300 ft from the assigned value. The correction was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a late crosscheck of the contour spacing and the spot elevations ahead, allowed the A/C to settle as the ground rose along the leg. SP detected the trend unprompted at about 200 ft below the assigned navigation altitude, referred to the MEF of the grid square and regained the altitude promptly. The remaining legs were flown with the relief checked ahead of the A/C.
texts.3: SP read the relief correctly from the contour lines, the spot elevations and the Maximum Elevation Figures and anticipated each change of terrain along the route. SP used the contour interval given in the legend and the gradient tints to confirm the terrain picture, keeping altitude within +/- 150 ft of the assigned navigation altitude. Terrain clearance over every grid square remained comfortably above the MEF.
texts.4: SP interpreted the relief continuously and had the MEF of each grid square and the relevant spot elevations available before entering it. SP used the contour spacing to predict the slope of the terrain ahead and held the assigned navigation altitude with negligible deviations. Terrain awareness required no prompting at any point of the route.
texts.marginal: SP interpreted the relief within standards, but the MEF and the spot elevations were consulted only after the terrain had visibly started to rise. The trend is toward a reactive rather than anticipatory use of the relief information, and SP is expected to read the contour interval and the MEF of the next grid square before entering it so that the altitude is set in advance.

error_modes.label: SYMBOL SIZE AND CHART SCALE LIMITATIONS
error_modes.source: technique:8.15 CHARTS (Navigational Charts, Scales, Chart Legend)

texts.0: SP, due to judging the real-world size of the features from the size of their symbols on the 1:500.000 sectional, expected a lookout tower and a minor airfield to be as conspicuous as symbols that cover about half a nautical mile and 4.000 ft to scale. SP did not appreciate that the discrepancies between the real world and its chart representation result from the limitations imposed by scale, with road widths alone exaggerated about 20 times, and rejected the correct checkpoints as non-matching. The position was lost and the IP took the A/C to re-establish the route, with heading more than 10 degrees off the briefed value.
texts.1: SP, due to expecting the ground features to match the exaggerated symbol sizes of the sectional, hesitated to accept a checkpoint that looked far smaller than the chart suggested. SP accepted the correct feature only after the IP verbally explained the scale exaggeration, and heading was at the 10 degrees limit when the identification was completed. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to comparing the apparent size of the ground feature with the size of its chart symbol, delayed the identification of a small airfield shown by an open circle. SP recalled unprompted that the symbol sizes do not conform to true scale while the relative positions of the features remain accurate, confirmed the checkpoint from the distance to a nearby road and continued on plan. Heading was held between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the delay.
texts.3: SP identified the checkpoints from the relative position of the features rather than from the size of the symbols, allowing for the exaggeration of the sectional symbology. SP used the accurate charted distances between objects to confirm each point and held heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. No correct feature was rejected because of its apparent size.
texts.4: SP treated the symbol sizes of the 1:500.000 sectional as conventions and worked entirely from the accurate relative positions and distances between the features. SP identified even the small and low-contrast checkpoints on first sight, with negligible deviations in heading, altitude and airspeed. The scale limitations of the chart never delayed an identification.
texts.marginal: SP allowed for the chart scale limitations within standards, but the first comparison was still made on apparent feature size and only then on the relative position of the objects. The trend is toward hesitation over small checkpoints whose symbols are large on the chart, and SP is expected to lead every identification with the charted distance to the neighbouring features.
